revision.text: Tsurugaoka is a shrine in Kamakura, Japan dedicated to warriors. It was constructed on the orders of Minamoto no Yoritomo, the founder of the Kamakura Shogunate.
'''Tsurugaoka''' is a shrine in [[Kamakura]], [[Japan]] dedicated to warriors. It was constructed on the orders of Minamoto no Yoritomo, the founder of the Kamakura Shogunate. {{Japan-stub}}

'''Tsurugaoka''' is a shrine in [[Kamakura]], [[Japan]]. It was constructed on the orders of Minamoto no Yoritomo, the founder of the Kamakura Shogunate, who invited Hachiman, the God of warriors to reside there and guard his government. {{Japan-stub}}

[[Image:TsurugaokaHachiman4269.jpg|thumb|right|250px|View down the stairs at Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine]] '''Tsurugaoka''' is a [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It was constructed on the orders of [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], who invited [[Hachiman]], the God of warriors, to reside there and guard his government.
[[Sakura|Cherry trees]] line the avenue to the shrine. The trees were also ordered by Yoritomo, as a prayer for the safe delivery of his first-born son.
''Yabusame'', archery from horseback, is practiced at the shrine.
[[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on February 13, 1219 by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands aside the great staircase at the shrine.
{{Japan-stub}} [[ja:鶴岡八幡宮]]

[[Image:TsurugaokaHachiman4269.jpg|thumb|right|250px|View down the stairs at Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine]] '''Tsurugaoka''' (鶴岡八幡宮) is the most important [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]].
It was originally built in [[1063]] near Yuigahama, and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ojin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]], the God of warriors, to reside there and guard his government.
There are a number of shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Ienari Tokugawa]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun.
[[Sakura|Cherry trees]] line the avenue to the shrine. The trees were ordered by Yoritomo as a prayer for the safe delivery of his first-born son. ''[[Yabusame]]'', archery from horseback, is practiced at the shrine.
[[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands aside the great staircase at the shrine.
{{Japan-stub}} [[Category:Shinto shrines]] [[ja:鶴岡八幡宮]]

[[Image:Large ginkgo in Tsurugaoka-hachimangu Shrine.jpg|thumb|Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine]]
'''Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine''' (鶴岡八幡宮, literally ''Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū'') is the most important [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]].
It was originally built in [[1063]] near [[Yuigahama]], and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ōjin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]], the god worshipped popularly among warriors, to reside there and guard his government.
There are a number of shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Ienari Tokugawa]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun.
[[Sakura|Cherry trees]] line the avenue to the shrine. The trees were ordered by Yoritomo as a prayer for the safe delivery of his first-born son. ''[[Yabusame]]'', archery from horseback, is practiced at the shrine.
[[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great staircase at the shrine.

{{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine

It was originally built in [[1063]] near [[Yuigahama]], and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ōjin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]], the god worshipped popularly among warriors, to reside there and guard his government. There are a number of shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great staircase at the shrine. == Tsurugaoka Hachiman before the Meiji era == Tsurugaoka Hachiman is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008. Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]{{cite book|last=Mutsu|first=Iso|title=Kamakura. Fact and Legend|publisher=Tuttle Publishing |date=1995/06|chapter=Jufuku-ji|isbn=ISBN 0804819688|url=http://www.amazon.com/Kamakura-Fact-Legend-Iso-Mutsu/dp/0804819688/ref=sr_1_1/102-3997530-9203357?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1207616602&sr=1-1 |language=English}}. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. == References == == External links == {{Commonscat|TsurugaokaHachimangu}} * [http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/ Official website (in Japanese)] * [http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/dgkeysearchdetail.cfm?trg=1&strucID=139733&imageID=110031&word=japan&s=1¬word=&d=&c=&f=&lWord=&lField=&sScope=&sLevel=&sLabel=&total=1807&num=372&imgs=12&pNum=&pos=382 New York Public Library Digital Gallery, early photograph of Shrine steps where Sanetomo was killed] {{coor title dms|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1500}} [[Category:1063 establishments]] [[Category:1190s architecture]] [[Category:1828 architecture]] [[Category:Kamakura, Kanagawa]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Religious organizations established in the 11th century]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kanagawa Prefecture]] [[de:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[es:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[fr:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[it:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[ja:鶴岡八幡宮]] [[th:ศาลเจ้าสึรุงะโอะกะ ฮะจิมัง]]

{{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine
鶴岡八幡宮 | image = Large ginkgo in Tsurugaoka-hachimangu Shrine.jpg | width = | caption = Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine | type = [[Hachiman Shrine]] | dedication = [[Hachiman]] | founded = 1063 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, [[Kamakura, Kanagawa]] | phone = 0467-22-0315 | website = http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html 鶴岡八幡宮 (in Japanese) }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine'''|鶴岡八幡宮|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū}} is the most important [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It was originally built in [[1063]] near [[Yuigahama]], and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ōjin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]], the god worshipped popularly among warriors, to reside there and guard his government. There are a number of shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Tokugawa Ienari]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun. [[Sakura|Cherry trees]] line the avenue to the shrine. The trees were ordered by Yoritomo as a prayer for the safe delivery of his first-born son. ''[[Yabusame]]'', archery from horseback, is practiced at the shrine. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great staircase at the shrine. == Tsurugaoka Hachiman before the Meiji era == Tsurugaoka Hachiman is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their properties{{nihongo|Kamakura Official Textbook for Culture and Tourism|鎌倉観光文化検定公式テキストブック}}, Kamakura Shunshūsha, 2008 {{ja icon}}. Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]{{cite book|last=Mutsu|first=Iso|title=Kamakura. Fact and Legend|publisher=Tuttle Publishing |date=1995/06|chapter=Jufuku-ji|isbn=ISBN 0804819688|url=http://www.amazon.com/Kamakura-Fact-Legend-Iso-Mutsu/dp/0804819688/ref=sr_1_1/102-3997530-9203357?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1207616602&sr=1-1 |language=English}}. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman has become impoverished as an unintended consequence of an imposed, overly-inflexible reform orthodoxy. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == References == == External links == {{Commonscat|TsurugaokaHachimangu}} * [http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/ Official website (in Japanese)] * New York Public Library Digital Gallery: Link to early photograph of Shrine steps where Sanetomo was killed (posted link failed, needing to be re-established) {{coor title dms|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1500}} [[Category:1063 establishments]] [[Category:1190s architecture]] [[Category:1828 architecture]] [[Category:Kamakura, Kanagawa]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Religious organizations established in the 11th century]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kanagawa Prefecture]] [[de:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[es:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[fr:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[it:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[ja:鶴岡八幡宮]] [[th:ศาลเจ้าสึรุงะโอะกะ ฮะจิมัง]]

Fact and Legend|publisher=Tuttle Publishing |date=1995/06|chapter=Jufuku-ji|isbn=ISBN 0804819688|url=http://www.amazon.com/Kamakura-Fact-Legend-Iso-Mutsu/dp/0804819688/ref=sr_1_1/102-3997530-9203357?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1207616602&sr=1-1 |language=English}}. In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony. {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine
鶴岡八幡宮 | image = Large ginkgo in Tsurugaoka-hachimangu Shrine.jpg | width = | caption = Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine | type = [[Hachiman Shrine]] | dedication = [[Hachiman]] | founded = 1063 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, [[Kamakura, Kanagawa]] | phone = 0467-22-0315 | website = http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html 鶴岡八幡宮 (in Japanese) }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine'''|鶴岡八幡宮|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū}} is the most important [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It was originally built in [[1063]] in [[Zaimokuza Beach|Zaimokuza]] where tiny [[Moto Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine]] now stands, and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ōjin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]], the god worshipped popularly among warriors, to reside there and guard his government. There are a number of shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Tokugawa Ienari]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun. Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[Yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and [[kyūdō]] (Japanese archery) are practiced at the shrine. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great staircase at the shrine. == Wakamiya Ōji== [[Image:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo| sandō|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in [[Yuigahama]] and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}} in Kyoto, Wakamiya Oji used to be much wider and flanked by pine trees{{nihongo|Kamakura Official Textbook for Culture and Tourism|鎌倉観光文化検定公式テキストブック}}, Kamakura Shunshūsha, 2008, pages 56-57 {{ja icon}}. Its name ("Young Prince Avenue") derives from its having been built as a prayer for the safe delivery of the shogun's first son. Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''Ichi no Torii'' (first gate), ''Ni no Torii'' (second gate) and ''San no Torii'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', lies the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine. == Tsurugaoka Hachiman before the Meiji era == Tsurugaoka Hachiman is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{en icon}}. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their properties{{nihongo|Kamakura Official Textbook for Culture and Tourism|鎌倉観光文化検定公式テキストブック}}, Kamakura Shunshūsha, 2008, page 28 {{ja icon}}. Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]{{cite book|last=Mutsu|first=Iso|title=Kamakura. Fact and Legend|publisher=Tuttle Publishing |date=1995/06|chapter=Jufuku-ji|isbn=ISBN 0804819688|url=http://www.amazon.com/Kamakura-Fact-Legend-Iso-Mutsu/dp/0804819688/ref=sr_1_1/102-3997530-9203357?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1207616602&sr=1-1 |language=English}}. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == References == == External links == {{Commonscat|TsurugaokaHachimangu}} * [http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/ Official website (in Japanese)] * New York Public Library Digital Gallery: Link to early photograph of Shrine steps where Sanetomo was killed (posted link failed, needing to be re-established) {{coor title dms|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1500}} [[Category:1063 establishments]] [[Category:1190s architecture]] [[Category:1828 architecture]] [[Category:Kamakura, Kanagawa]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Religious organizations established in the 11th century]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kanagawa Prefecture]] [[de:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[es:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[fr:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[it:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[ja:鶴岡八幡宮]] [[th:ศาลเจ้าสึรุงะโอะกะ ฮะจิมัง]]

Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]{{cite book|last=Mutsu|first=Iso|title=Kamakura. Fact and Legend|publisher=Tuttle Publishing |date=1995/06|chapter=Jufuku-ji|isbn=ISBN 0804819688|url=http://www.amazon.com/Kamakura-Fact-Legend-Iso-Mutsu/dp/0804819688/ref=sr_1_1/102-3997530-9203357?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1207616602&sr=1-1 |language=English}}. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == References == == External links == {{Commonscat|TsurugaokaHachimangu}} * [http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/ Official website (in Japanese)] * New York Public Library Digital Gallery: Link to early photograph of Shrine steps where Sanetomo was killed (posted link failed, needing to be re-established) {{coor title dms|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1500}} [[Category:1063 establishments]] [[Category:1190s architecture]] [[Category:1828 architecture]] [[Category:Kamakura, Kanagawa]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Religious organizations established in the 11th century]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kanagawa Prefecture]] [[de:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[es:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[fr:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[it:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[ja:鶴岡八幡宮]] [[th:ศาลเจ้าสึรุงะโอะกะ ฮะจิมัง]]

What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == Notes == == References == * {{cite book | last = Kamiya | first = Michinori | coauthors = | title = Fukaku Aruku - Kamakura Shiseki Sansaku | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | date = 2000/08 | location = [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]] | language = Japanese | id = ISBN 4774003409 }} * {{cite book | last = Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo | first = | coauthors = | title = Kamakura Kankō Bunka Kentei Kōshiki Tekisutobukku | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | date = 2008 | location = Kamakura | language = Japanese | id = ISBN 978-4-7740-0386-3 }} == External links == {{Commonscat|TsurugaokaHachimangu}} * [http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/ Official website (in Japanese)] * New York Public Library Digital Gallery: Link to early photograph of Shrine steps where Sanetomo was killed (posted link failed, needing to be re-established) {{coor title dms|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1500}} [[Category:1063 establishments]] [[Category:1190s architecture]] [[Category:1828 architecture]] [[Category:Kamakura, Kanagawa]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Religious organizations established in the 11th century]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kanagawa Prefecture]] [[de:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[es:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[fr:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[it:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[ja:鶴岡八幡宮]] [[th:ศาลเจ้าสึรุงะโอะกะ ฮะจิมัง]]

{{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū
鶴岡八幡宮 | image = Large ginkgo in Tsurugaoka-hachimangu Shrine.jpg | width = | caption = The stairway to the ''haiden'' | type = [[Hachiman Shrine]] | dedication = [[Hachiman]] | founded = 1063 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, [[Kamakura, Kanagawa]] | phone = 0467-22-0315 | website = http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū'''|鶴岡八幡宮}} is the most important [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. It was originally built in [[1063]] in [[Zaimokuza]] where tiny [[Moto Hachiman ]] now stands, and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ōjin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]], the god worshipped popularly among warriors, to reside there and guard his government. There are a number of shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Tokugawa Ienari]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun. Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[Yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and [[kyūdō]] (Japanese archery) are practiced at the shrine. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great staircase at the shrine. == Wakamiya Ōji== [[Image:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo| sandō|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in [[Yuigahama]] and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}. Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print)Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57). Its name ("Young Prince Avenue") derives from its having been built as a prayer for the safe delivery of the shogun's first son. Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''Ichi no Torii'' (first gate), ''Ni no Torii'' (second gate) and ''San no Torii'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine.　 == Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū before the Meiji era == [[Image:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|250 px|Tsurugaoka Hachiman--gū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period]] Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{en icon}}. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their propertiesKamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28). Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]{{cite book|last=Mutsu|first=Iso|title=Kamakura. Fact and Legend|publisher=Tuttle Publishing |date=1995/06|chapter=Jufuku-ji|isbn=ISBN 0804819688|url=http://www.amazon.com/Kamakura-Fact-Legend-Iso-Mutsu/dp/0804819688/ref=sr_1_1/102-3997530-9203357?ie=UTF8&s=books&qid=1207616602&sr=1-1 |language=English}}. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. Its huge {{nihongo|''sanmon''|山門}} gate is now at [[Kōmyō-ji]] and is even now the largest in the Kanto areaKamiya (2006/08: 189 -190) In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == Notes == == References == * {{cite book | last = Kamiya | first = Michinori | coauthors = | title = Fukaku Aruku - Kamakura Shiseki Sansaku Vol. 1 | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | date = 2000/08 | location = [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]] | language = Japanese | id = ISBN 4774003409 }} * {{cite book | last = Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo | first = | coauthors = | title = Kamakura Kankō Bunka Kentei Kōshiki Tekisutobukku | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | date = 2008 | location = Kamakura | language = Japanese | id = ISBN 978-4-7740-0386-3 }} == External links == {{Commonscat|TsurugaokaHachimangu}} * [http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/ Official website (in Japanese)] * New York Public Library Digital Gallery: Link to early photograph of Shrine steps where Sanetomo was killed (posted link failed, needing to be re-established) {{coor title dms|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1500}} [[Category:1063 establishments]] [[Category:1190s architecture]] [[Category:1828 architecture]] [[Category:Kamakura, Kanagawa]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Religious organizations established in the 11th century]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kanagawa Prefecture]] [[de:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[es:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[fr:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[it:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[ja:鶴岡八幡宮]] [[th:ศาลเจ้าสึรุงะโอะกะ ฮะจิมัง]]

{{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū
鶴岡八幡宮 | image = Large ginkgo in Tsurugaoka-hachimangu Shrine.jpg | width = | caption = The stairway to the ''haiden'' | type = [[Hachiman Shrine]] | dedication = [[Hachiman]] | founded = 1063 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, [[Kamakura, Kanagawa]] | phone = 0467-22-0315 | website = http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū'''|鶴岡八幡宮}} is the most important [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. == Structure == The shrine, which used to be also a Buddhist temple and far bigger than today, was originally built in [[1063]] in [[Zaimokuza]] where tiny [[Moto Hachiman ]] now stands, and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ōjin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]], the god worshiped popularly among warriors, to reside there and guard his government. Today, after the first ''torii'' there are three small bridges, two flat and one arched. In the days of the shogunate there used to be only two, a normal one and another arched, made in wood and painted red. The shogun would leave his retinue there and proceed alone on foot to the shrineMutsu (1995/06: 100). The arched bridge was called ''Akabashi'' (''Red Bridge''), and was reserved to him: common people had to use the flat one. The bridges span over a canal that joins together two ponds popularly called {{nihongo|''Genpei-ike''|源平池}}, or "Genpei ponds". The term comes from the names of two families, the Minamoto ("Gen") and the Taira ("Pei"), that fought each other in Yoritomo's day. The ponds were built by Yoritomo's wife [[Hōjō Masako|Masako]] at the time of the war between the clans and the number of islands they contain carried a grim symbolism. The right hand one is the largest and contains just three: three in Japanese is "san", which is also one reading of the character for "life". The smaller taira pond contains four: four in Japanese is "shi", the same word as death. The color of the lotuses used to be white in the Minamoto pond and blood-red red in the Taira pond, two colors which were also those of the respective family flags. One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was removed in 1868 at the time of the ''Shinto and Buddhism separation'' order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956Kamiya (2008: 18 - 19). There are a number of shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Tokugawa Ienari]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun. Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[Yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and [[kyūdō]] (Japanese archery) are practiced at the shrine. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great staircase at the shrine. The great tree is over 1000 years old. == Wakamiya Ōji== [[Image:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo| sandō|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in [[Yuigahama]] and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}. Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print)Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57). Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''Ichi no Torii'' (first gate), ''Ni no Torii'' (second gate) and ''San no Torii'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine.　 == Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū before the Meiji era == [[Image:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|250 px|Tsurugaoka Hachiman--gū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period]] Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their propertiesKamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28). Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]Mutsu (1995/06:174. Its huge {{nihongo|''sanmon''|山門}} gate visible in the Edo period print is at [[Kōmyō-ji]] and is even now the largest in the [[Kanto]] areaKamiya (2006/08: 189 -190) In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. The smaller taira pond contains four: four in Japanese is "shi", the same word as death. The color of the lotuses used to be white in the Minamoto pond and blood-red red in the Taira pond, two colors which were also those of the respective family flags. One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was removed in 1868 at the time of the ''Shinto and Buddhism separation'' order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956Kamiya (2008: 18 - 19). There are a number of shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Tokugawa Ienari]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun. Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[Yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and [[kyūdō]] (Japanese archery) are practiced at the shrine. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great staircase at the shrine. The great tree is over 1000 years old. == Wakamiya Ōji== [[Image:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo| sandō|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in [[Yuigahama]] and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}. Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print)Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57). Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''Ichi no Torii'' (first gate), ''Ni no Torii'' (second gate) and ''San no Torii'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine.　 == Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū before the Meiji era == [[Image:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|250 px|Tsurugaoka Hachiman--gū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period]] Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{en icon}}. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their propertiesKamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28). Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]Mutsu (1995/06:174. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. Its huge {{nihongo|''sanmon''|山門}} gate visible in the Edo period print is at [[Kōmyō-ji]] and is even now the largest in the [[Kanto]] areaKamiya (2006/08: 189 -190) In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū
鶴岡八幡宮 | image = Large ginkgo in Tsurugaoka-hachimangu Shrine.jpg | width = | caption = The stairway to the ''haiden'' | type = [[Hachiman Shrine]] | dedication = [[Hachiman]] | founded = 1063 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, [[Kamakura, Kanagawa]] | phone = 0467-22-0315 | website = http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū'''|鶴岡八幡宮}} is the most important [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. == Structure == The shrine, which used to be also a Buddhist temple and far bigger than today, was originally built in [[1063]] in [[Zaimokuza]] where tiny [[Moto Hachiman ]] now stands, and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ōjin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]], the god worshiped popularly among warriors, to reside there and guard his government. Today, after the first ''torii'' there are three small bridges, two flat and one arched. In the days of the shogunate there used to be only two, a normal one and another arched, made in wood and painted red. The shogun would leave his retinue there and proceed alone on foot to the shrineMutsu (1995/06: 100). The arched bridge was called ''Akabashi'' (''Red Bridge''), and was reserved to him: common people had to use the flat one. The bridges span over a canal that joins together two ponds popularly called {{nihongo|''Genpei-ike''|源平池}}, or "Genpei ponds". The term comes from the names of two families, the Minamoto ("Gen") and the Taira ("Pei"), that fought each other in Yoritomo's day. The ponds were built by Yoritomo's wife [[Hōjō Masako|Masako]] at the time of the war between the clans and the number of islands they contain carried a grim symbolism. The right hand one is the largest and contains just three: three in Japanese is "san", which is also one reading of the character for "life". The smaller Taira pond contains four: four in Japanese is "shi", the same word as death. The color of the lotuses used to be white in the Minamoto pond and blood-red red in the Taira pond, two colors which were also those of the respective family flags. One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was removed in 1868 at the time of the ''Shinto and Buddhism separation'' order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956Kamiya (2008: 18 - 19). There are a number of shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Tokugawa Ienari]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun. Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[Yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and [[kyūdō]] (Japanese archery) are practiced at the shrine. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great staircase at the shrine. The great tree is over 1000 years old. == Wakamiya Ōji== [[Image:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo| sandō|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in [[Yuigahama]] and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}. Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print)Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57). Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''Ichi no Torii'' (first gate), ''Ni no Torii'' (second gate) and ''San no Torii'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine.　 == Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū before the Meiji era == [[Image:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|250 px|Tsurugaoka Hachiman--gū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period]] Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{en icon}}. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their propertiesKamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28). Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]Mutsu (1995/06:174. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. Its huge {{nihongo|''sanmon''|山門}} gate visible in the Edo period print is at [[Kōmyō-ji]] and is even now the largest in the [[Kanto]] areaKamiya (2006/08: 189 -190) In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == Notes == == References == * {{cite book | last = Mutsu | first = Iso | coauthors = | title = Kamakura. The stele just after and to the left of the first ''torii'' saysOriginal Japanese text available [[http://www.kcn-net.org/sisekihi/genpei.htm here]]:
The Genpei Ponds
The Azuma Kagami says that "In April 1182 Minamoto no Yoritomo told to monk Senkō and to Ōba Kageyoshi to have two ponds dug within the shrine." According to another version of the story, it was Yoritomo's wife [[Hōjō Masako|Masako]] who, to pray for the prosperity of the Minamoto family, had these ponds dug, and had white lotuses planted in the east one and read ones in the west one, colors which are those of the Taira and Minamoto clans. From this derives their name.
[[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] by an archer hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great staircase at the shrine. The great tree is over 1000 years old. Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[Yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and [[kyūdō]] (Japanese archery) are practiced at the shrine. == Wakamiya Ōji== [[Image:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo| sandō|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in [[Yuigahama]] and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}. Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print)Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57). Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''Ichi no Torii'' (first gate), ''Ni no Torii'' (second gate) and ''San no Torii'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine.　 == Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū before the Meiji era == [[Image:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|250 px|Tsurugaoka Hachiman--gū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period]] Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{en icon}}. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their propertiesKamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28). Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]Mutsu (1995/06:174. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. Its huge {{nihongo|''sanmon''|山門}} gate visible in the Edo period print is at [[Kōmyō-ji]] and is even now the largest in the [[Kanto]] areaKamiya (2006/08: 189 -190) In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū
鶴岡八幡宮 | image = Large ginkgo in Tsurugaoka-hachimangu Shrine.jpg | width = | caption = The stairway to the ''haiden'' | type = [[Hachiman Shrine]] | dedication = [[Hachiman]] | founded = 1063 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, [[Kamakura, Kanagawa]] | phone = 0467-22-0315 | website = http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū'''|鶴岡八幡宮}} is the most important [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. == Structure == This shrine, which used to be also a Buddhist temple and far bigger than today, was originally built in [[1063]] in [[Zaimokuza]] where tiny [[Moto Hachiman ]] now stands, and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ōjin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]], the god worshiped popularly among warriors, to reside there and guard his government. As one enters, after the first ''[[torii]]'' (Shinto gate) there are three small bridges, two flat on the sides and one arched at the center. In the days of the shogunate there used to be only two, a normal one and another arched, made in wood and painted red. The shogun would leave his retinue there and proceed alone on foot to the shrineMutsu (1995/06: 100). The arched bridge was called ''Akabashi'' (''Red Bridge''), and was reserved to him: common people had to use the flat one. The bridges span over a canal that joins together two ponds popularly called {{nihongo|''Genpei-ike''|源平池}}, or "Genpei ponds". The term comes from the names of the two families, the Minamoto ("Gen") and the Taira ("Pei"), that fought each other in Yoritomo's day. The stele just after and to the left of the first ''torii'' explains what's the origin of the nameOriginal Japanese text available [[http://www.kcn-net.org/sisekihi/genpei.htm here]]:
The Genpei Ponds
The Azuma Kagami says that "In April 1182 Minamoto no Yoritomo told to monk Senkō and to Ōba Kageyoshi to have two ponds dug within the shrine." According to another version of the story, it was Yoritomo's wife [[Hōjō Masako|Masako]] who, to pray for the prosperity of the Minamoto family, had these ponds dug, and had white lotuses planted in the east one and read ones in the west one, colors which are those of the Taira and Minamoto clans. From this derives their name.
The red of those lotuses is supposed to stand for the spilled blood of the TairaKamiya (2008: 18 - 19). One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was removed in 1868 at the time of the ''Shinto and Buddhism separation'' order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956Kamiya (2008: 18 - 19). There are a number of sub-shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Tokugawa Ienari]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] with an arrow by his nephew Minamoto no Kokio (1200-1219) who was hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great stairway at the shrine. The great tree is over 1000 years old. Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[Yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and [[kyūdō]] (Japanese archery) are practiced at the shrine. == Wakamiya Ōji== [[Image:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo| sandō|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in [[Yuigahama]] and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}, Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print)Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57). Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''Ichi no Torii'' (first gate), ''Ni no Torii'' (second gate) and ''San no Torii'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine.　 == Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū before the Meiji era == [[Image:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|250 px|Tsurugaoka Hachiman--gū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period. In the lower right corner, tiny [[Moto Hachiman]]]] Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{en icon}}. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their propertiesKamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28). Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]Mutsu (1995/06:174. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. Its huge {{nihongo|''sanmon''|山門}} gate visible in the Edo period print is at [[Kōmyō-ji]] and is even now the largest in the [[Kanto]] areaKamiya (2006/08: 189 -190) In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == Notes == == References == * {{cite book | last = Mutsu | first = Iso | coauthors = | title = Kamakura. Fact and Legend | publisher = Tuttle Publishing | date = 1995/06 | location = Tokyo | language = English | id = ISBN 0804819688 }} * {{cite book | last = Kamiya | first = Michinori | coauthors = | title = Fukaku Aruku - Kamakura Shiseki Sansaku Vol. 1 | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | date = 2000/08 | location = [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]] | language = Japanese | id = ISBN 4774003409 }} * {{cite book | last = Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo | first = | coauthors = | title = Kamakura Kankō Bunka Kentei Kōshiki Tekisutobukku | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | date = 2008 | location = Kamakura | language = Japanese | id = ISBN 978-4-7740-0386-3 }} == External links == {{Commonscat|TsurugaokaHachimangu}} * [http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/ Official website (in Japanese)] * [[National Archives of Japan]], Digital Gallery: ** Mori Koan map: [http://jpimg.digital.archives.go.jp/jpg_prg/jgmWeb.dll?TmpFileDisp4?si=0&md=0&ql=10&env=jpeg2k_images/ezu/nihonyochizu/148_soshukamakura_e.env&l=8&cy=4567&cx=4731&dy=400&dx=600&i=lossy/kouseisai/ezu/nihonyochizu/148_soshukamakura.jp2&file=temp_kuniezu_e.html Soshu Kamakuranozu], drawn in 5th year of ''[[Horeki]]'' (1755). * [[New York Public Library]] Digital Gallery: ** NYPL ID 119488, unknown photographer, albumen print, 189?-190?: [http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/id?119488 Perspective beyond torii] ** NYPL ID 118907, [[Felice Beato]], albumen print, 187?: [http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/id?118907 Shrine steps and forecourt] ** NYPL ID 110031, [[Kimbei Kusakabe]], albumen print, 188?-189? [http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/id?110031 Great stairway] ** NYPL ID 118911, [[Felice Beato]], albumen print, 187?: [http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/id?118911 Senior Shrine structural detail] ** NYPL ID 118912, [[Felice Beato]], albumen print, 187?: [http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/id?118912 ''Tahōtō,'' single-storied pagoda] {{coor title dms|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP_type:landmark_scale:1500}} [[Category:1063 establishments]] [[Category:1190s architecture]] [[Category:1828 architecture]] [[Category:Kamakura, Kanagawa]] [[Category:National Treasures of Japan]] [[Category:Religious organizations established in the 11th century]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kanagawa Prefecture]] [[de:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[es:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[fr:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū]] [[it:Santuario Tsurugaoka Hachiman]] [[ja:鶴岡八幡宮]] [[th:ศาลเจ้าสึรุงะโอะกะ ฮะจิมัง]]

According to another version of the story, it was Yoritomo's wife [[Hōjō Masako|Masako]] who, to pray for the prosperity of the Minamoto family, had these ponds dug, and had white lotuses planted in the east one and read ones in the west one, colors which are those of the Taira and Minamoto clans. From this derives their name.
The red of those lotuses is supposed to stand for the spilled blood of the TairaKamiya (2008: 18 - 19). One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was removed in 1868 at the time of the ''Shinto and Buddhism separation'' order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956Kamiya (2008: 18 - 19). There are a number of sub-shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Tokugawa Ienari]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] with an arrow by his nephew Minamoto no Kokio (1200-1219) who was hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great stairway at the shrine. The great tree is over 1000 years old. Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[Yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and [[kyūdō]] (Japanese archery) are practiced at the shrine. == Wakamiya Ōji== [[Image:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo| sandō|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in [[Yuigahama]] and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}, Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print)Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57). Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''Ichi no Torii'' (first gate), ''Ni no Torii'' (second gate) and ''San no Torii'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine.　 == Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū before the Meiji era == [[Image:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|250 px|Tsurugaoka Hachiman--gū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period. In the lower right corner, tiny [[Moto Hachiman]]]] Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{en icon}}. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their propertiesKamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28). Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]Mutsu (1995/06:174. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. Its huge {{nihongo|''sanmon''|山門}} gate visible in the Edo period print is at [[Kōmyō-ji]] and is even now the largest in the [[Kanto]] areaKamiya (2006/08: 189 -190) In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == Notes == == References == * {{cite book | last = Mutsu | first = Iso | coauthors = | title = Kamakura. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == Notes == == References == * {{cite book | last = Mutsu | first = Iso | coauthors = | title = Kamakura. {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū
鶴岡八幡宮 | image = Large ginkgo in Tsurugaoka-hachimangu Shrine.jpg | width = | caption = The stairway to the ''haiden'' | type = [[Hachiman Shrine]] | dedication = [[Hachiman]] | founded = 1063 | closed = | founder = | priest = | address = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, [[Kamakura, Kanagawa]] | phone = 0467-22-0315 | website = http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū'''|鶴岡八幡宮}} is the most important [[Jinja (shrine)|shrine]] in the city of [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]], [[Kanagawa Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. == Structure == This shrine, which used to be also a Buddhist temple and far bigger than today, was originally built in [[1063]] in [[Zaimokuza]] where tiny [[Moto Hachiman ]] now stands, and was dedicated to the [[Emperor Ōjin]], his mother [[Jingu_of_Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the [[Kamakura shogunate]], moved it to its present location in [[1191]] and invited [[Hachiman]]A ''kami'' is transferred to a new location through a process called [[kanjō]]., the god worshiped popularly among warriors, to reside there and guard his government. Both the shrine and the city were built with [[Fung Shui]] in mind. The present location was carefully chosen as the most propitious after consultation with a [[diviner]] because it had a mountain to the north (the {{nihongo|''Hokuzan''|北山}}), a river to the east (the [[Namerigawa]]), a great road to the west (the {{nihongo|''Kotō Kaidō''|古東街道}}) and was open to the south (on [[Sagami Bay]])Ōnuki (2008:80). Each direction was protected by a god: [[Black Tortoise|Genbu]] guarded the north, [[Azure Dragon|Seiryū]] the east, [[White Tiger (Chinese constellation)|Byakko]] the west and [[Vermilion Bird|Suzaku]] the south. The [[willows]] near the Genpei Ponds (see below) and the [[catalpa]]s next to the Museum of Modern Art represent respectively Seiryū and Byakko. In spite of all the changes the shrine has gone through over the years, in this respect Yoritomo's design is still basically intact. As one enters, after the first ''[[torii]]'' (Shinto gate) there are three small bridges, two flat on the sides and one arched at the center. In the days of the shogunate there used to be only two, a normal one and another arched, made in wood and painted red. The shogun would leave his retinue there and proceed alone on foot to the shrineMutsu (1995/06: 100). The arched bridge was called ''Akabashi'' (''Red Bridge''), and was reserved to him: common people had to use the flat one. The bridges span over a canal that joins together two ponds popularly called {{nihongo|''Genpei-ike''|源平池}}, or "Genpei ponds". The term comes from the names of the two families, the Minamoto ("Gen") and the Taira ("Pei"), that fought each other in Yoritomo's day. The stele just after and to the left of the first ''torii'' explains what's the origin of the nameOriginal Japanese text available [[http://www.kcn-net.org/sisekihi/genpei.htm here]]:
The Genpei Ponds
The Azuma Kagami says that "In April 1182 Minamoto no Yoritomo told to monk Senkō and to Ōba Kageyoshi to have two ponds dug within the shrine." According to another version of the story, it was Yoritomo's wife [[Hōjō Masako|Masako]] who, to pray for the prosperity of the Minamoto family, had these ponds dug, and had white lotuses planted in the east one and read ones in the west one, colors which are those of the Taira and Minamoto clans. From this derives their name.
The red of those lotuses is supposed to stand for the spilled blood of the TairaKamiya (2008: 18 - 19). One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was removed in 1868 at the time of the ''Shinto and Buddhism separation'' order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956Kamiya (2008: 18 - 19). There are a number of sub-shrines on the site, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in [[1828]] by [[Tokugawa Ienari]], the 11th [[Tokugawa_shogunate|Tokugawa]] shogun. [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]], the third Kamakura [[shogun]], was assassinated on [[February 13]], [[1219]] with an arrow by his nephew Minamoto no Kokio (1200-1219) who was hiding behind the great [[ginkgo]] tree that still stands beside the great stairway at the shrine. The great tree is over 1000 years old. Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[Yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and [[kyūdō]] (Japanese archery) are practiced at the shrine. == Wakamiya Ōji== [[Image:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo| sandō|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in [[Yuigahama]] and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}, Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print below)Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57). Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''Ichi no Torii'' (first gate), ''Ni no Torii'' (second gate) and ''San no Torii'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|Geba|下馬}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders would get off their horses in deference to the temple. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine.　 == Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū before the Meiji era == [[Image:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|250 px|Tsurugaoka Hachiman--gū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period. In the lower right corner, tiny [[Moto Hachiman]]]] Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name used to be {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and Shinto had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{en icon}}. The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their propertiesKamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28). Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|[[Niō]]|仁王}}] (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to [[Jufuku-ji]], where they still areSee article [[Jufuku-ji]]Mutsu (1995/06:174. The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|''tahōtō''|多宝塔}} tower, its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂}}, and its {{nihongo|''garan''|伽藍}}. Its huge {{nihongo|''sanmon''|山門}} gate visible in the Edo period print is at [[Kōmyō-ji]] and is even now the largest in the [[Kanto]] areaKamiya (2006/08: 189 -190) In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. == Notes == == References == * {{cite book | last = Mutsu | first = Iso | coauthors = | title = Kamakura. Fact and Legend | publisher = Tuttle Publishing | date = 1995/06 | location = Tokyo | language = English | id = ISBN 0804819688 }} * {{cite book | last = Kamiya | first = Michinori | coauthors = | title = Fukaku Aruku - Kamakura Shiseki Sansaku Vol. 1 | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | date = 2000/08 | location = [[Kamakura, Kanagawa|Kamakura]] | language = Japanese | id = ISBN 4774003409 }} * {{cite book | last = Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo | first = | coauthors = | title = Kamakura Kankō Bunka Kentei Kōshiki Tekisutobukku | publisher = Kamakura Shunshūsha | date = 2008 | location = Kamakura | language = Japanese | id = ISBN 978-4-7740-0386-3 }} * {{cite book |last=Ōnuki |first=Akihiko |title=Kamakura. Rekishi to Fushigi wo Aruku |publisher=Jitsugyō no Nihonsha |location=Tokyo |date=2008 |isbn=978-4-408-59306-7 |language=Japanese }} == External links == {{Commonscat|TsurugaokaHachimangu}} * [http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/ Official website (in Japanese)] * [[National Archives of Japan]], Digital Gallery: ** Mori Koan map: [http://jpimg.digital.archives.go.jp/jpg_prg/jgmWeb.dll?TmpFileDisp4?si=0&md=0&ql=10&env=jpeg2k_images/ezu/nihonyochizu/148_soshukamakura_e.env&l=8&cy=4567&cx=4731&dy=400&dx=600&i=lossy/kouseisai/ezu/nihonyochizu/148_soshukamakura.jp2&file=temp_kuniezu_e.html Soshu Kamakuranozu], drawn in 5th year of ''[[Horeki]]'' (1755). * [[New York Public Library]] Digital Gallery: ** NYPL ID 119488, unknown photographer, albumen print, 189?-190?: [http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/id?119488 Perspective beyond torii] ** NYPL ID 118907, [[Felice Beato]], albumen print, 187?: [http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/id?118907 Shrine steps and forecourt] ** NYPL ID 110031, [[Kimbei Kusakabe]], albumen print, 188?-189?
