{{lang|ja|鶴岡八幡宮}} | image = TsurugaokaHachiman-M8867.jpg | caption = The approach to the Senior Shrine (''hongū''). | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP-14_type:landmark_scale:1500|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Hachiman shrine|Hachiman Shrine]] | deity = [[Hachiman]] | founded_by = | established = 1063 | date_destroyed = | location = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}} | website = {{URL|http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachimangū'''|鶴岡八幡宮}} is the most important {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} in the city of {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}, {{ill|Kanagawa Prefecture|en|Kanagawa Prefecture|WD=Q127513|lt=Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}. The shrine is a cultural center of the city of Kamakura and serves as the venue of many of its most important festivals with two museums. For most of its history, it served both as a [[Hachiman shrine|Hachiman Shrine]], and in latter years a {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temple}} typical of {{ill|Japanese Buddhist architecture|en|Japanese Buddhist architecture|WD=Q7883744|lt=Japanese Buddhist architecture}}. The famed Buddhist priest [[:en:Nichiren Daishonin|Nichiren Daishonin]] once reputedly visited the shrine to reprimand the [[kami]] [[Hachiman]] just before his execution at {{ill|Shichirigahama|en|Shichirigahama|WD=Q7496115|lt=Shichirigahama}} beach. A former one thousand-year-old {{ill|Ginkgo biloba|en|Ginkgo biloba|WD=Q43284|lt=ginkgo tree}} near its entrance was uprooted by a storm on 10 March 2010. The shrine continues to serve as one of the {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}. ==History== This shrine was originally built in 1063 as a branch of [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Shrine]] in {{ill|Zaimokuza|en|Zaimokuza|WD=Q121432378|lt=Zaimokuza}} where tiny [[Moto Hachiman]] now stands and dedicated to the {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Emperor Ōjin}}, (deified with the name [[Hachiman]], tutelary ''[[kami]]'' of warriors), his mother [[:en:Jingu of Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}, moved it to its present location in 1191 and invited [[Hachiman]]A ''kami'' is transferred to a new location through a process called [[kanjō]]. to reside in the new location to protect his government. The shrine caught a major fire in 14 November 1280, where several artifacts were also stolen from the inner sanctum of the shrine. === Assassination of Minamoto no Sanetomo === One of the historical events the shrine is tied to is the assassination of Sanetomo, last of Minamoto no Yoritomo's sons. Under heavy snow on the evening of February 12, 1219 ({{ill|Jōkyū|en|Jōkyū|WD=Q1195428|lt=Jōkyū}} 1, 26th day of the 1st month),Gregorian date obtained directly from the original Nengō using [https://uni-tuebingen.de/geschichte-japans/nengo_calc.htm Nengocalc] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930014735/http://www.uni-tuebingen.de/geschichte-japans/nengo_calc.htm |date=2007-09-30 }} shōgun [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]] was coming down from Tsurugaoka Hachimangū's Senior Shrine after assisting to a ceremony celebrating his nomination to [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]]. His nephew [[:en:Kugyō (Minamoto no Yoshinari)|Kugyō]], son of second shōgun [[Minamoto no Yoriie]], came out from next to the stone stairway of the shrine, then suddenly attacked and assassinated him in the hope to become ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' himself.Azuma Kagami; Mutsu (1995/06: 102–104) The killer is often described as hiding behind the giant ginkgo, but no contemporary text mentions the tree, and this detail is likely an {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo-period}} invention first appeared in {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}}'s {{ill|Shinpen Kamakurashi|en|Shinpen Kamakurashi|WD=Q2397169|lt=Shinpen Kamakurashi}}. For his act Kugyō was himself beheaded a few hours later, thus bringing the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}} line of the Minamoto clan and their rule in Kamakura to a sudden end. === Shrine and temple === [[File:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|left|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period. Clearly visible its many Buddhist temples, later destroyed. In the lower right corner, tiny [[Moto Hachiman]]]]Tsurugaoka Hachimangū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name was {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and ''kami'' worship in shrine-temple complexes like Tsurugaoka called ''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji}}'' had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change.[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{in lang|en}} (According to the ''[[honji suijaku]]'' theory, Japanese ''kami'' were just local manifestations of universal {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddhas}}, and Hachiman in particular was one of the earliest and most popular syncretic gods. Already in the 7th century, for example in {{ill|Usa, Ōita|en|Usa, Ōita|WD=Q114147|lt=Usa}}, Kyūshū, Hachiman was worshiped together with Miroku Bosatsu ([[Maitreya]]).Bernhard Scheid) The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their properties.Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28) Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|{{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}}|仁王}}} (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to {{ill|Jufuku-ji|en|Jufuku-ji|WD=Q167087|lt=Jufuku-ji}}, where they still are.See article {{ill|Jufuku-ji|en|Jufuku-ji|WD=Q167087|lt=Jufuku-ji}}Mutsu (1995/06:174) The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|[[shichidō garan]]|七堂伽藍}} (a complete seven-building Buddhist temple compound), its ''[[tahōtō]]'' tower, and its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂|enshrinement hall (of a {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddha}})}}. In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachimangū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji Era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. ===Meiji-Showa periods=== From 1871 through 1946, Tsurugaoka was officially designated one of the {{nihongo|''[[:en:Kokuhei-chūsha|Kokuhei-chūsha]]''|国幣中社}}, meaning that it stood in the mid-range of [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines|Ranked, nationally significant shrines]]. == Layout of shrine complex == [[File:TsurugaokaHachiman-M8808.jpg|thumb|left|Torii at entrance to shrine. The arched bridge is visible to the right.]] Both the shrine and the city were built with [[:en:Feng Shui|Feng Shui]] in mind. The present location was carefully chosen as the most propitious after consulting a [[:en:Diviner|Diviner]] because it had a mountain to the north (the {{nihongo|''Hokuzan''|北山}}), a river to the east (the [[Namerikawa (Kanagawa)|Namerikawa]]), a great road to the west (the {{nihongo|''Kotō Kaidō''|古東街道}}) and was open to the south (on {{ill|Sagami Bay|en|Sagami Bay|WD=Q1061221|lt=Sagami Bay}}).Ōnuki (2008:80) Each direction was protected by a god: [[:en:Black Tortoise|Genbu]] guarded the north, {{ill|Azure Dragon|en|Azure Dragon|WD=Q515882|lt=Seiryū}} the east, [[:en:White Tiger (Chinese constellation)|Byakko]] the west and {{ill|Vermilion Bird|en|Vermilion Bird|WD=Q1059392|lt=Suzaku}} the south. The [[:en:Willows|Willows]] near the Genpei Ponds (see below) and the [[catalpa]]s next to the [http://www.moma.pref.kanagawa.jp/en/public/HallTop.do?hl=k Museum of Modern Art] represent respectively Seiryū and Byakko. In spite of all the changes the shrine has gone through over the years, in this respect Yoritomo's design is still basically intact. [[File:Tsurugaoka Hachimangu From Third Torii until First Torii.jpg|thumb|Three large torii on the approach (sandō) of shrine]] There is a 1.8 km straight street in the front of shrine, called "{{ill|Wakamiya Ōji|en|Wakamiya Ōji|WD=Q7960797|lt=Wakamiya Ōji}} (若宮大路)". It is the approach ({{ill|Sandō|en|Sandō|WD=Q667783|lt=Sandō}} (参道)) of Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū, there are three big [[Torii]] (Shinto gate). The Torii gate farthest from the shrine is called Ichi-no-Torii (the first torii), the one in the middle is Ni-no-Torii (the second torii) and the one in front of the shrine is [[Wakamiya Ōji#San no Torii|San-no-Torii]] (the third torii). As one enters, after San-no-Torii (the third torii) there are three small bridges, two flat ones on the sides and an arched one at the center. In the days of the shogunate there used to be only two, a normal one and another arched, made in wood and painted red. The shōgun would leave his retinue there and proceed alone on foot to the shrine.Mutsu (1995/06: 102-104) The arched bridge was called ''Akabashi'' (''Red Bridge''), and was reserved to him: common people had to use the flat one. The bridges span over a canal that joins two ponds popularly called {{nihongo|''Genpei-ike''|源平池}}, or "Genpei ponds". The term comes from the names of the two families, the Minamoto ("Gen") and the Taira ("Pei"), that fought each other in Yoritomo's day. The stele just after and to the left of the first ''torii'' explains the origin of the name:Original Japanese text available [http://www.kcn-net.org/sisekihi/genpei.htm here]
The Genpei Ponds
File:Genpei-ike 01.JPG|Genpei ponds (Minamoto Pond) File:Genpei-ike 02.JPG|Genpei ponds (Taira Pond) The Azuma Kagami says that "In April 1182 Minamoto no Yoritomo told monk Senkō and Ōba Kageyoshi to have two ponds dug within the shrine." According to another version of the story, it was Yoritomo's wife {{ill|Hōjō Masako|en|Hōjō Masako|WD=Q463961|lt=Masako}} who, to pray for the prosperity of the Minamoto family, had these ponds dug, and had white lotuses planted in the east one and red ones in the west one, colors which are those of the Taira and Minamoto clans. From this derives their name.
The red of those lotuses is supposed to stand for the spilled blood of the Taira.Kamiya (2008: 17 - 23) ===Sub-shrines and infrastructures=== [[File:Yui-Wakamiya.jpg|thumb|The Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo, where one can pray at [[:en:Yui Wakamiya|Yui Wakamiya]] without actually going there.]] [[File:Maiden stage.jpg|thumb|left|Music performance at ''Maiden'']] Tsurugaoka Hachimangū includes several sub-shrines, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine ({{nihongo|''Wakamiya''|若宮}}) at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine ({{nihongo|''Hongū''|本宮}}) 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in 1828 by {{ill|Tokugawa Ienari|en|Tokugawa Ienari|WD=Q439717|lt=Tokugawa Ienari}}, the 11th [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa]] ''shōgun'' in the ''{{ill|Hachiman-zukuri|en|Hachiman-zukuri|WD=Q3125455|lt=Hachiman-zukuri}}'' style.{{cite book|last=Bocking|first=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto - 'Hachiman-zukuri' |year=1997|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-7007-1051-5}} Right under the stairway there's an open pavilion called {{nihongo|''Maiden''|舞殿}} where weddings, dances and music are performed. A couple of hundred meters to the right of the Junior Shrine lies {{nihongo|''Shirahata Jinja''|Shirahata Shrine}}, a {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|WD=Q1139795|lt=National Treasure}}. To the left of the Senior Shrine lies {{nihongo|''Maruyama'' {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|WD=Q514480|lt=Inari shrine}}|丸山稲荷社}} with its many ''torii''. Near ''Shirahata Jinja'' one can also find the {{nihongo|''Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo''|由比若宮遥拝所}}, literally the "Yui Wakamiya Pray-at-a-Distance Place" (see photo). This facility, originally created for the ''shōgun'''s benefit, allows one to worship at distant [[:en:Yui Wakamiya|Yui Wakamiya]] ([[Moto Hachiman]]) without actually going all the way to {{ill|Zaimokuza|en|Zaimokuza|WD=Q121432378|lt=Zaimokuza}}.[http://www.kcn-net.org/e_kama_history/komachi_yukinoshita/area1_1.htm Komachi, Nishi Mikado], by the Kamakura Citizen's Network, retrieved on July 23, 2008 Right next to the ''Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo'' there are two stones: pouring water on them should reveal on each the contour of a turtle. One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine called {{nihongo|''Hataage Benzaiten'' Shrine|旗上弁財天社}} dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was dismantled in 1868 at the time of the "Shinto and Buddhism separation" order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956. ===Wakamiya Ōji=== [[File:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo|{{ill|Sandō|en|Sandō|WD=Q667783|lt=Sandō}}|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in {{ill|Yuigahama|en|Yuigahama|WD=Q8060490|lt=Yuigahama}} and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}, Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print below).Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57) Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#Ichi no Torii|Ichi no Torii]]'' (first gate), ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#Ni no Torii|Ni no Torii]]'' (second gate) and ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#San no Torii|San no Torii]]'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|[[Wakamiya Ōji#Geba Yotsukado|Geba Yotsukado]]|下馬四つ角}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders had to get off their horses in deference to [[Hachiman]] and his shrine. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine. ===Giant ginkgo=== [[File:Giant Ginkgo in Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|left|The giant ginkgo before its uprooting]] [[File:Ginkgo-reborn-2.jpg|right|thumb|The stump of the fallen ginkgo has produced leaves]] The {{ill|Ginkgo biloba|en|Ginkgo biloba|WD=Q43284|lt=ginkgo}} tree that stood next to Tsurugaoka Hachimangū's stairway almost from its foundation and which appears in almost every old print of the shrine was completely uprooted and greatly damaged at 4:40 in the morning on March 10, 2010. According to an expert who analyzed the tree, the fall is likely due to rot. Both the tree's stump and a section of its trunk replanted nearby have produced leaves (see photo). The tree was nicknamed {{nihongo|''kakure-ichō''|隠れ銀杏|hiding ginkgo}} because according to an {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} {{ill|Urban legend|en|Urban legend|WD=Q189349|lt=Urban legend}}, a now-famous assassin hid behind it before striking his victim. For details, see the article {{ill|Shinpen Kamakurashi|en|Shinpen Kamakurashi|WD=Q2397169|lt=Shinpen Kamakurashi}}. ==Activities== [[File:Kamakura Yabusame.jpg|thumb|''Yabusame'' at Tsurugaoka Hachimangū]] Tsurugaoka Hachimangū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and ''[[kyūdō]]'' (Japanese archery) are practiced within the shrine. It also has extensive {{ill|Peony|en|Peony|WD=Q147105|lt=Peony}} gardens, three coffee shops, a kindergarten, offices and a ''[[:en:Dōjō|Dōjō]]''. Within its grounds stand two museums, the {{ill|Kamakura Museum of National Treasures|en|Kamakura Museum of National Treasures|WD=Q3330314|lt=Kamakura Museum of National Treasures}}, owned by the City of Kamakura, and the prefectural [http://www.moma.pref.kanagawa.jp/en/public/HallTop.do?hl=k Museum of Modern Art]. ==Gallery of shrines== File:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū Shrine.jpg|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū {{lang|ja|鶴岡八幡宮}} | image = TsurugaokaHachiman-M8867.jpg | caption = The approach to the Senior Shrine (''hongū''). | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP-14_type:landmark_scale:1500|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Hachiman shrine|Hachiman Shrine]] | deity = [[Hachiman]] | founded_by = | established = 1063 | date_destroyed = | location = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}} | website = {{URL|http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachimangū'''|鶴岡八幡宮}} is the most important {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} in the city of {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}, {{ill|Kanagawa Prefecture|en|Kanagawa Prefecture|WD=Q127513|lt=Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}. The shrine is a cultural center of the city of Kamakura and serves as the venue of many of its most important festivals with two museums. For most of its history, it served both as a [[Hachiman shrine|Hachiman Shrine]], and in latter years a {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temple}} typical of {{ill|Japanese Buddhist architecture|en|Japanese Buddhist architecture|WD=Q7883744|lt=Japanese Buddhist architecture}}. The famed Buddhist priest [[:en:Nichiren Daishonin|Nichiren Daishonin]] once reputedly visited the shrine to reprimand the [[kami]] [[Hachiman]] just before his execution at {{ill|Shichirigahama|en|Shichirigahama|WD=Q7496115|lt=Shichirigahama}} beach. A former one thousand-year-old {{ill|Ginkgo biloba|en|Ginkgo biloba|WD=Q43284|lt=ginkgo tree}} near its entrance was uprooted by a storm on 10 March 2010. The shrine continues to serve as one of the {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}. ==History== This shrine was originally built in 1063 as a branch of [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Shrine]] in {{ill|Zaimokuza|en|Zaimokuza|WD=Q121432378|lt=Zaimokuza}} where tiny [[Moto Hachiman]] now stands and dedicated to the {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Emperor Ōjin}}, (deified with the name [[Hachiman]], tutelary ''[[kami]]'' of warriors), his mother [[:en:Jingu of Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}, moved it to its present location in 1191 and invited [[Hachiman]]A ''kami'' is transferred to a new location through a process called [[kanjō]]. to reside in the new location to protect his government. The shrine caught a major fire in 14 November 1280, where several artifacts were also stolen from the inner sanctum of the shrine. === Assassination of Minamoto no Sanetomo === One of the historical events the shrine is tied to is the assassination of Sanetomo, last of Minamoto no Yoritomo's sons. Under heavy snow on the evening of February 12, 1219 ({{ill|Jōkyū|en|Jōkyū|WD=Q1195428|lt=Jōkyū}} 1, 26th day of the 1st month),Gregorian date obtained directly from the original Nengō using [https://uni-tuebingen.de/geschichte-japans/nengo_calc.htm Nengocalc] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930014735/http://www.uni-tuebingen.de/geschichte-japans/nengo_calc.htm |date=2007-09-30 }} shōgun [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]] was coming down from Tsurugaoka Hachimangū's Senior Shrine after assisting to a ceremony celebrating his nomination to [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]]. His nephew [[:en:Kugyō (Minamoto no Yoshinari)|Kugyō]], son of second shōgun [[Minamoto no Yoriie]], came out from next to the stone stairway of the shrine, then suddenly attacked and assassinated him in the hope to become ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' himself.Azuma Kagami; Mutsu (1995/06: 102–104) The killer is often described as hiding behind the giant ginkgo, but no contemporary text mentions the tree, and this detail is likely an {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo-period}} invention first appeared in {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}}'s {{ill|Shinpen Kamakurashi|en|Shinpen Kamakurashi|WD=Q2397169|lt=Shinpen Kamakurashi}}. For his act Kugyō was himself beheaded a few hours later, thus bringing the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}} line of the Minamoto clan and their rule in Kamakura to a sudden end. === Shrine and temple === [[File:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|left|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period. Clearly visible its many Buddhist temples, later destroyed. In the lower right corner, tiny [[Moto Hachiman]]]]Tsurugaoka Hachimangū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name was {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and ''kami'' worship in shrine-temple complexes like Tsurugaoka called ''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji}}'' had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change.[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{in lang|en}} (According to the ''[[honji suijaku]]'' theory, Japanese ''kami'' were just local manifestations of universal {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddhas}}, and Hachiman in particular was one of the earliest and most popular syncretic gods. Already in the 7th century, for example in {{ill|Usa, Ōita|en|Usa, Ōita|WD=Q114147|lt=Usa}}, Kyūshū, Hachiman was worshiped together with Miroku Bosatsu ([[Maitreya]]).Bernhard Scheid) The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their properties.Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28) Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|{{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}}|仁王}}} (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to {{ill|Jufuku-ji|en|Jufuku-ji|WD=Q167087|lt=Jufuku-ji}}, where they still are.See article {{ill|Jufuku-ji|en|Jufuku-ji|WD=Q167087|lt=Jufuku-ji}}Mutsu (1995/06:174) The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|[[shichidō garan]]|七堂伽藍}} (a complete seven-building Buddhist temple compound), its ''[[tahōtō]]'' tower, and its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂|enshrinement hall (of a {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddha}})}}. In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachimangū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji Era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. ===Meiji-Showa periods=== From 1871 through 1946, Tsurugaoka was officially designated one of the {{nihongo|''[[:en:Kokuhei-chūsha|Kokuhei-chūsha]]''|国幣中社}}, meaning that it stood in the mid-range of [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines|Ranked, nationally significant shrines]]. == Layout of shrine complex == [[File:TsurugaokaHachiman-M8808.jpg|thumb|left|Torii at entrance to shrine. The arched bridge is visible to the right.]] Both the shrine and the city were built with [[:en:Feng Shui|Feng Shui]] in mind. The present location was carefully chosen as the most propitious after consulting a [[:en:Diviner|Diviner]] because it had a mountain to the north (the {{nihongo|''Hokuzan''|北山}}), a river to the east (the [[Namerikawa (Kanagawa)|Namerikawa]]), a great road to the west (the {{nihongo|''Kotō Kaidō''|古東街道}}) and was open to the south (on {{ill|Sagami Bay|en|Sagami Bay|WD=Q1061221|lt=Sagami Bay}}).Ōnuki (2008:80) Each direction was protected by a god: [[:en:Black Tortoise|Genbu]] guarded the north, {{ill|Azure Dragon|en|Azure Dragon|WD=Q515882|lt=Seiryū}} the east, [[:en:White Tiger (Chinese constellation)|Byakko]] the west and {{ill|Vermilion Bird|en|Vermilion Bird|WD=Q1059392|lt=Suzaku}} the south. The [[:en:Willows|Willows]] near the Genpei Ponds (see below) and the [[catalpa]]s next to the [http://www.moma.pref.kanagawa.jp/en/public/HallTop.do?hl=k Museum of Modern Art] represent respectively Seiryū and Byakko. In spite of all the changes the shrine has gone through over the years, in this respect Yoritomo's design is still basically intact. [[File:Tsurugaoka Hachimangu From Third Torii until First Torii.jpg|thumb|Three large torii on the approach (sandō) of shrine]] There is a 1.8 km straight street in the front of shrine, called "{{ill|Wakamiya Ōji|en|Wakamiya Ōji|WD=Q7960797|lt=Wakamiya Ōji}} (若宮大路)". It is the approach ({{ill|Sandō|en|Sandō|WD=Q667783|lt=Sandō}} (参道)) of Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū, there are three big [[Torii]] (Shinto gate). The Torii gate farthest from the shrine is called Ichi-no-Torii (the first torii), the one in the middle is Ni-no-Torii (the second torii) and the one in front of the shrine is [[Wakamiya Ōji#San no Torii|San-no-Torii]] (the third torii). As one enters, after San-no-Torii (the third torii) there are three small bridges, two flat ones on the sides and an arched one at the center. In the days of the shogunate there used to be only two, a normal one and another arched, made in wood and painted red. The shōgun would leave his retinue there and proceed alone on foot to the shrine.Mutsu (1995/06: 102-104) The arched bridge was called ''Akabashi'' (''Red Bridge''), and was reserved to him: common people had to use the flat one. The bridges span over a canal that joins two ponds popularly called {{nihongo|''Genpei-ike''|源平池}}, or "Genpei ponds". The term comes from the names of the two families, the Minamoto ("Gen") and the Taira ("Pei"), that fought each other in Yoritomo's day. The stele just after and to the left of the first ''torii'' explains the origin of the name:Original Japanese text available [http://www.kcn-net.org/sisekihi/genpei.htm here]
The Genpei Ponds
File:Genpei-ike 01.JPG|Genpei ponds (Minamoto Pond) File:Genpei-ike 02.JPG|Genpei ponds (Taira Pond) The Azuma Kagami says that "In April 1182 Minamoto no Yoritomo told monk Senkō and Ōba Kageyoshi to have two ponds dug within the shrine." According to another version of the story, it was Yoritomo's wife {{ill|Hōjō Masako|en|Hōjō Masako|WD=Q463961|lt=Masako}} who, to pray for the prosperity of the Minamoto family, had these ponds dug, and had white lotuses planted in the east one and red ones in the west one, colors which are those of the Taira and Minamoto clans. From this derives their name.
The red of those lotuses is supposed to stand for the spilled blood of the Taira.Kamiya (2008: 17 - 23) ===Sub-shrines and infrastructures=== [[File:Yui-Wakamiya.jpg|thumb|The Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo, where one can pray at [[:en:Yui Wakamiya|Yui Wakamiya]] without actually going there.]] [[File:Maiden stage.jpg|thumb|left|Music performance at ''Maiden'']] Tsurugaoka Hachimangū includes several sub-shrines, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine ({{nihongo|''Wakamiya''|若宮}}) at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine ({{nihongo|''Hongū''|本宮}}) 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in 1828 by {{ill|Tokugawa Ienari|en|Tokugawa Ienari|WD=Q439717|lt=Tokugawa Ienari}}, the 11th [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa]] ''shōgun'' in the ''{{ill|Hachiman-zukuri|en|Hachiman-zukuri|WD=Q3125455|lt=Hachiman-zukuri}}'' style.{{cite book|last=Bocking|first=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto - 'Hachiman-zukuri' |year=1997|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-7007-1051-5}} Right under the stairway there's an open pavilion called {{nihongo|''Maiden''|舞殿}} where weddings, dances and music are performed. A couple of hundred meters to the right of the Junior Shrine lies {{nihongo|''Shirahata Jinja''|Shirahata Shrine}}, a {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|WD=Q1139795|lt=National Treasure}}. To the left of the Senior Shrine lies {{nihongo|''Maruyama'' {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|WD=Q514480|lt=Inari shrine}}|丸山稲荷社}} with its many ''torii''. Near ''Shirahata Jinja'' one can also find the {{nihongo|''Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo''|由比若宮遥拝所}}, literally the "Yui Wakamiya Pray-at-a-Distance Place" (see photo). This facility, originally created for the ''shōgun'''s benefit, allows one to worship at distant [[:en:Yui Wakamiya|Yui Wakamiya]] ([[Moto Hachiman]]) without actually going all the way to {{ill|Zaimokuza|en|Zaimokuza|WD=Q121432378|lt=Zaimokuza}}.[http://www.kcn-net.org/e_kama_history/komachi_yukinoshita/area1_1.htm Komachi, Nishi Mikado], by the Kamakura Citizen's Network, retrieved on July 23, 2008 Right next to the ''Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo'' there are two stones: pouring water on them should reveal on each the contour of a turtle. One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine called {{nihongo|''Hataage Benzaiten'' Shrine|旗上弁財天社}} dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was dismantled in 1868 at the time of the "Shinto and Buddhism separation" order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956. ===Wakamiya Ōji=== [[File:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo|{{ill|Sandō|en|Sandō|WD=Q667783|lt=Sandō}}|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in {{ill|Yuigahama|en|Yuigahama|WD=Q8060490|lt=Yuigahama}} and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}, Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print below).Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57) Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#Ichi no Torii|Ichi no Torii]]'' (first gate), ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#Ni no Torii|Ni no Torii]]'' (second gate) and ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#San no Torii|San no Torii]]'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|[[Wakamiya Ōji#Geba Yotsukado|Geba Yotsukado]]|下馬四つ角}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders had to get off their horses in deference to [[Hachiman]] and his shrine. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine. ===Giant ginkgo=== [[File:Giant Ginkgo in Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|left|The giant ginkgo before its uprooting]] [[File:Ginkgo-reborn-2.jpg|right|thumb|The stump of the fallen ginkgo has produced leaves]] The {{ill|Ginkgo biloba|en|Ginkgo biloba|WD=Q43284|lt=ginkgo}} tree that stood next to Tsurugaoka Hachimangū's stairway almost from its foundation and which appears in almost every old print of the shrine was completely uprooted and greatly damaged at 4:40 in the morning on March 10, 2010. According to an expert who analyzed the tree, the fall is likely due to rot. Both the tree's stump and a section of its trunk replanted nearby have produced leaves (see photo). The tree was nicknamed {{nihongo|''kakure-ichō''|隠れ銀杏|hiding ginkgo}} because according to an {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} {{ill|Urban legend|en|Urban legend|WD=Q189349|lt=Urban legend}}, a now-famous assassin hid behind it before striking his victim. For details, see the article {{ill|Shinpen Kamakurashi|en|Shinpen Kamakurashi|WD=Q2397169|lt=Shinpen Kamakurashi}}. ==Activities== [[File:Kamakura Yabusame.jpg|thumb|''Yabusame'' at Tsurugaoka Hachimangū]] Tsurugaoka Hachimangū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and ''[[kyūdō]]'' (Japanese archery) are practiced within the shrine. It also has extensive {{ill|Peony|en|Peony|WD=Q147105|lt=Peony}} gardens, three coffee shops, a kindergarten, offices and a ''[[:en:Dōjō|Dōjō]]''. Within its grounds stand two museums, the {{ill|Kamakura Museum of National Treasures|en|Kamakura Museum of National Treasures|WD=Q3330314|lt=Kamakura Museum of National Treasures}}, owned by the City of Kamakura, and the prefectural [http://www.moma.pref.kanagawa.jp/en/public/HallTop.do?hl=k Museum of Modern Art]. ==Gallery of shrines== File:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū Shrine.jpg|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū {{lang|ja|鶴岡八幡宮}} | image = TsurugaokaHachiman-M8867.jpg | caption = The approach to the Senior Shrine (''hongū''). | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP-14_type:landmark_scale:1500|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Hachiman shrine|Hachiman Shrine]] | deity = [[Hachiman]] | founded_by = | established = 1063 | date_destroyed = | location = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}} | website = {{URL|http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachimangū'''|鶴岡八幡宮}} is the most important {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} in the city of {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}, {{ill|Kanagawa Prefecture|en|Kanagawa Prefecture|WD=Q127513|lt=Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}. The shrine is a cultural center of the city of Kamakura and serves as the venue of many of its most important festivals with two museums. For most of its history, it served both as a [[Hachiman shrine|Hachiman Shrine]], and in latter years a {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temple}} typical of {{ill|Japanese Buddhist architecture|en|Japanese Buddhist architecture|WD=Q7883744|lt=Japanese Buddhist architecture}}. The famed Buddhist priest [[:en:Nichiren Daishonin|Nichiren Daishonin]] once reputedly visited the shrine to reprimand the [[kami]] [[Hachiman]] just before his execution at {{ill|Shichirigahama|en|Shichirigahama|WD=Q7496115|lt=Shichirigahama}} beach. A former one thousand-year-old {{ill|Ginkgo biloba|en|Ginkgo biloba|WD=Q43284|lt=ginkgo tree}} near its entrance was uprooted by a storm on 10 March 2010. The shrine continues to serve as one of the {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}. ==History== This shrine was originally built in 1063 as a branch of [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Shrine]] in {{ill|Zaimokuza|en|Zaimokuza|WD=Q121432378|lt=Zaimokuza}} where tiny [[Moto Hachiman]] now stands and dedicated to the {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Emperor Ōjin}}, (deified with the name [[Hachiman]], tutelary ''[[kami]]'' of warriors), his mother [[:en:Jingu of Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}, moved it to its present location in 1191 and invited [[Hachiman]]A ''kami'' is transferred to a new location through a process called [[kanjō]]. to reside in the new location to protect his government. The shrine caught a major fire in 14 November 1280, where several artifacts were also stolen from the inner sanctum of the shrine. === Assassination of Minamoto no Sanetomo === One of the historical events the shrine is tied to is the assassination of Sanetomo, last of Minamoto no Yoritomo's sons. Under heavy snow on the evening of February 12, 1219 ({{ill|Jōkyū|en|Jōkyū|WD=Q1195428|lt=Jōkyū}} 1, 26th day of the 1st month),Gregorian date obtained directly from the original Nengō using [https://uni-tuebingen.de/geschichte-japans/nengo_calc.htm Nengocalc] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930014735/http://www.uni-tuebingen.de/geschichte-japans/nengo_calc.htm |date=2007-09-30 }} shōgun [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]] was coming down from Tsurugaoka Hachimangū's Senior Shrine after assisting to a ceremony celebrating his nomination to [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]]. His nephew [[:en:Kugyō (Minamoto no Yoshinari)|Kugyō]], son of second shōgun [[Minamoto no Yoriie]], came out from next to the stone stairway of the shrine, then suddenly attacked and assassinated him in the hope to become ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' himself.Azuma Kagami; Mutsu (1995/06: 102–104) The killer is often described as hiding behind the giant ginkgo, but no contemporary text mentions the tree, and this detail is likely an {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo-period}} invention first appeared in {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}}'s {{ill|Shinpen Kamakurashi|en|Shinpen Kamakurashi|WD=Q2397169|lt=Shinpen Kamakurashi}}. For his act Kugyō was himself beheaded a few hours later, thus bringing the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}} line of the Minamoto clan and their rule in Kamakura to a sudden end. === Shrine and temple === [[File:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|left|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period. Clearly visible its many Buddhist temples, later destroyed. In the lower right corner, tiny [[Moto Hachiman]]]]Tsurugaoka Hachimangū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name was {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and ''kami'' worship in shrine-temple complexes like Tsurugaoka called ''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji}}'' had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change.[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{in lang|en}} (According to the ''[[honji suijaku]]'' theory, Japanese ''kami'' were just local manifestations of universal {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddhas}}, and Hachiman in particular was one of the earliest and most popular syncretic gods. Already in the 7th century, for example in {{ill|Usa, Ōita|en|Usa, Ōita|WD=Q114147|lt=Usa}}, Kyūshū, Hachiman was worshiped together with Miroku Bosatsu ([[Maitreya]]).Bernhard Scheid) The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their properties.Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28) Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|{{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}}|仁王}}} (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to {{ill|Jufuku-ji|en|Jufuku-ji|WD=Q167087|lt=Jufuku-ji}}, where they still are.See article {{ill|Jufuku-ji|en|Jufuku-ji|WD=Q167087|lt=Jufuku-ji}}Mutsu (1995/06:174) The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|[[shichidō garan]]|七堂伽藍}} (a complete seven-building Buddhist temple compound), its ''[[tahōtō]]'' tower, and its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂|enshrinement hall (of a {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddha}})}}. In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachimangū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji Era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. ===Meiji-Showa periods=== From 1871 through 1946, Tsurugaoka was officially designated one of the {{nihongo|''[[:en:Kokuhei-chūsha|Kokuhei-chūsha]]''|国幣中社}}, meaning that it stood in the mid-range of [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines|Ranked, nationally significant shrines]]. == Layout of shrine complex == [[File:TsurugaokaHachiman-M8808.jpg|thumb|left|Torii at entrance to shrine. The arched bridge is visible to the right.]] Both the shrine and the city were built with [[:en:Feng Shui|Feng Shui]] in mind. The present location was carefully chosen as the most propitious after consulting a [[:en:Diviner|Diviner]] because it had a mountain to the north (the {{nihongo|''Hokuzan''|北山}}), a river to the east (the [[Namerikawa (Kanagawa)|Namerikawa]]), a great road to the west (the {{nihongo|''Kotō Kaidō''|古東街道}}) and was open to the south (on {{ill|Sagami Bay|en|Sagami Bay|WD=Q1061221|lt=Sagami Bay}}).Ōnuki (2008:80) Each direction was protected by a god: [[:en:Black Tortoise|Genbu]] guarded the north, {{ill|Azure Dragon|en|Azure Dragon|WD=Q515882|lt=Seiryū}} the east, [[:en:White Tiger (Chinese constellation)|Byakko]] the west and {{ill|Vermilion Bird|en|Vermilion Bird|WD=Q1059392|lt=Suzaku}} the south. The [[:en:Willows|Willows]] near the Genpei Ponds (see below) and the [[catalpa]]s next to the [http://www.moma.pref.kanagawa.jp/en/public/HallTop.do?hl=k Museum of Modern Art] represent respectively Seiryū and Byakko. In spite of all the changes the shrine has gone through over the years, in this respect Yoritomo's design is still basically intact. [[File:Tsurugaoka Hachimangu From Third Torii until First Torii.jpg|thumb|Three large torii on the approach (sandō) of shrine]] There is a 1.8 km straight street in the front of shrine, called "{{ill|Wakamiya Ōji|en|Wakamiya Ōji|WD=Q7960797|lt=Wakamiya Ōji}} (若宮大路)". It is the approach ({{ill|Sandō|en|Sandō|WD=Q667783|lt=Sandō}} (参道)) of Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū, there are three big [[Torii]] (Shinto gate). The Torii gate farthest from the shrine is called Ichi-no-Torii (the first torii), the one in the middle is Ni-no-Torii (the second torii) and the one in front of the shrine is [[Wakamiya Ōji#San no Torii|San-no-Torii]] (the third torii). As one enters, after San-no-Torii (the third torii) there are three small bridges, two flat ones on the sides and an arched one at the center. In the days of the shogunate there used to be only two, a normal one and another arched, made in wood and painted red. The shōgun would leave his retinue there and proceed alone on foot to the shrine.Mutsu (1995/06: 102-104) The arched bridge was called ''Akabashi'' (''Red Bridge''), and was reserved to him: common people had to use the flat one. The bridges span over a canal that joins two ponds popularly called {{nihongo|''Genpei-ike''|源平池}}, or "Genpei ponds". The term comes from the names of the two families, the Minamoto ("Gen") and the Taira ("Pei"), that fought each other in Yoritomo's day. The stele just after and to the left of the first ''torii'' explains the origin of the name:Original Japanese text available [http://www.kcn-net.org/sisekihi/genpei.htm here]
The Genpei Ponds
File:Genpei-ike 01.JPG|Genpei ponds (Minamoto Pond) File:Genpei-ike 02.JPG|Genpei ponds (Taira Pond) The Azuma Kagami says that "In April 1182 Minamoto no Yoritomo told monk Senkō and Ōba Kageyoshi to have two ponds dug within the shrine." According to another version of the story, it was Yoritomo's wife {{ill|Hōjō Masako|en|Hōjō Masako|WD=Q463961|lt=Masako}} who, to pray for the prosperity of the Minamoto family, had these ponds dug, and had white lotuses planted in the east one and red ones in the west one, colors which are those of the Taira and Minamoto clans. From this derives their name.
The red of those lotuses is supposed to stand for the spilled blood of the Taira.Kamiya (2008: 17 - 23) ===Sub-shrines and infrastructures=== [[File:Yui-Wakamiya.jpg|thumb|The Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo, where one can pray at [[:en:Yui Wakamiya|Yui Wakamiya]] without actually going there.]] [[File:Maiden stage.jpg|thumb|left|Music performance at ''Maiden'']] Tsurugaoka Hachimangū includes several sub-shrines, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine ({{nihongo|''Wakamiya''|若宮}}) at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine ({{nihongo|''Hongū''|本宮}}) 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in 1828 by {{ill|Tokugawa Ienari|en|Tokugawa Ienari|WD=Q439717|lt=Tokugawa Ienari}}, the 11th [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa]] ''shōgun'' in the ''{{ill|Hachiman-zukuri|en|Hachiman-zukuri|WD=Q3125455|lt=Hachiman-zukuri}}'' style.{{cite book|last=Bocking|first=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto - 'Hachiman-zukuri' |year=1997|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-7007-1051-5}} Right under the stairway there's an open pavilion called {{nihongo|''Maiden''|舞殿}} where weddings, dances and music are performed. A couple of hundred meters to the right of the Junior Shrine lies {{nihongo|''Shirahata Jinja''|Shirahata Shrine}}, a {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|WD=Q1139795|lt=National Treasure}}. To the left of the Senior Shrine lies {{nihongo|''Maruyama'' {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|WD=Q514480|lt=Inari shrine}}|丸山稲荷社}} with its many ''torii''. Near ''Shirahata Jinja'' one can also find the {{nihongo|''Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo''|由比若宮遥拝所}}, literally the "Yui Wakamiya Pray-at-a-Distance Place" (see photo). This facility, originally created for the ''shōgun'''s benefit, allows one to worship at distant [[:en:Yui Wakamiya|Yui Wakamiya]] ([[Moto Hachiman]]) without actually going all the way to {{ill|Zaimokuza|en|Zaimokuza|WD=Q121432378|lt=Zaimokuza}}.[http://www.kcn-net.org/e_kama_history/komachi_yukinoshita/area1_1.htm Komachi, Nishi Mikado], by the Kamakura Citizen's Network, retrieved on July 23, 2008 Right next to the ''Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo'' there are two stones: pouring water on them should reveal on each the contour of a turtle. One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine called {{nihongo|''Hataage Benzaiten'' Shrine|旗上弁財天社}} dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was dismantled in 1868 at the time of the "Shinto and Buddhism separation" order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956. ===Wakamiya Ōji=== [[File:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo|{{ill|Sandō|en|Sandō|WD=Q667783|lt=Sandō}}|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in {{ill|Yuigahama|en|Yuigahama|WD=Q8060490|lt=Yuigahama}} and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}, Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print below).Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57) Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#Ichi no Torii|Ichi no Torii]]'' (first gate), ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#Ni no Torii|Ni no Torii]]'' (second gate) and ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#San no Torii|San no Torii]]'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|[[Wakamiya Ōji#Geba Yotsukado|Geba Yotsukado]]|下馬四つ角}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders had to get off their horses in deference to [[Hachiman]] and his shrine. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine. ===Giant ginkgo=== [[File:Giant Ginkgo in Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|left|The giant ginkgo before its uprooting]] [[File:Ginkgo-reborn-2.jpg|right|thumb|The stump of the fallen ginkgo has produced leaves]] The {{ill|Ginkgo biloba|en|Ginkgo biloba|WD=Q43284|lt=ginkgo}} tree that stood next to Tsurugaoka Hachimangū's stairway almost from its foundation and which appears in almost every old print of the shrine was completely uprooted and greatly damaged at 4:40 in the morning on March 10, 2010. According to an expert who analyzed the tree, the fall is likely due to rot. Both the tree's stump and a section of its trunk replanted nearby have produced leaves (see photo). The tree was nicknamed {{nihongo|''kakure-ichō''|隠れ銀杏|hiding ginkgo}} because according to an {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} {{ill|Urban legend|en|Urban legend|WD=Q189349|lt=Urban legend}}, a now-famous assassin hid behind it before striking his victim. For details, see the article {{ill|Shinpen Kamakurashi|en|Shinpen Kamakurashi|WD=Q2397169|lt=Shinpen Kamakurashi}}. ==Activities== [[File:Kamakura Yabusame.jpg|thumb|''Yabusame'' at Tsurugaoka Hachimangū]] Tsurugaoka Hachimangū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and ''[[kyūdō]]'' (Japanese archery) are practiced within the shrine. It also has extensive {{ill|Peony|en|Peony|WD=Q147105|lt=Peony}} gardens, three coffee shops, a kindergarten, offices and a ''[[:en:Dōjō|Dōjō]]''. Within its grounds stand two museums, the {{ill|Kamakura Museum of National Treasures|en|Kamakura Museum of National Treasures|WD=Q3330314|lt=Kamakura Museum of National Treasures}}, owned by the City of Kamakura, and the prefectural [http://www.moma.pref.kanagawa.jp/en/public/HallTop.do?hl=k Museum of Modern Art]. ==Gallery of shrines== File:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū Shrine.jpg|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū – a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} with {{ill|Buddhist architecture|en|Buddhist architecture|WD=Q2047562|lt=Buddhist architecture}} File:Inner court of Tsurugaoka {{lang|ja|鶴岡八幡宮}} | image = TsurugaokaHachiman-M8867.jpg | caption = The approach to the Senior Shrine (''hongū''). | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|35|19|29|N|139|33|21|E|region:JP-14_type:landmark_scale:1500|display=title,inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Hachiman shrine|Hachiman Shrine]] | deity = [[Hachiman]] | founded_by = | established = 1063 | date_destroyed = | location = 2-1-31 Yukinoshita, {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}} | website = {{URL|http://www.hachimangu.or.jp/index2.html}} | architecture_style = | festival = | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Tsurugaoka Hachimangū'''|鶴岡八幡宮}} is the most important {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} in the city of {{ill|Kamakura|en|Kamakura|WD=Q200267|lt=Kamakura}}, {{ill|Kanagawa Prefecture|en|Kanagawa Prefecture|WD=Q127513|lt=Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}. The shrine is a cultural center of the city of Kamakura and serves as the venue of many of its most important festivals with two museums. For most of its history, it served both as a [[Hachiman shrine|Hachiman Shrine]], and in latter years a {{ill|Tendai|en|Tendai|WD=Q855964|lt=Tendai}} {{ill|Buddhist temples in Japan|en|Buddhist temples in Japan|WD=Q3141900|lt=Buddhist temple}} typical of {{ill|Japanese Buddhist architecture|en|Japanese Buddhist architecture|WD=Q7883744|lt=Japanese Buddhist architecture}}. The famed Buddhist priest [[:en:Nichiren Daishonin|Nichiren Daishonin]] once reputedly visited the shrine to reprimand the [[kami]] [[Hachiman]] just before his execution at {{ill|Shichirigahama|en|Shichirigahama|WD=Q7496115|lt=Shichirigahama}} beach. A former one thousand-year-old {{ill|Ginkgo biloba|en|Ginkgo biloba|WD=Q43284|lt=ginkgo tree}} near its entrance was uprooted by a storm on 10 March 2010. The shrine continues to serve as one of the {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|en|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Property (Japan)}}. ==History== This shrine was originally built in 1063 as a branch of [[Iwashimizu Hachimangū|Iwashimizu Shrine]] in {{ill|Zaimokuza|en|Zaimokuza|WD=Q121432378|lt=Zaimokuza}} where tiny [[Moto Hachiman]] now stands and dedicated to the {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|WD=Q317997|lt=Emperor Ōjin}}, (deified with the name [[Hachiman]], tutelary ''[[kami]]'' of warriors), his mother [[:en:Jingu of Japan|Empress Jingu]] and his wife Hime-gami. [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]], the founder of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate}}, moved it to its present location in 1191 and invited [[Hachiman]]A ''kami'' is transferred to a new location through a process called [[kanjō]]. to reside in the new location to protect his government. The shrine caught a major fire in 14 November 1280, where several artifacts were also stolen from the inner sanctum of the shrine. === Assassination of Minamoto no Sanetomo === One of the historical events the shrine is tied to is the assassination of Sanetomo, last of Minamoto no Yoritomo's sons. Under heavy snow on the evening of February 12, 1219 ({{ill|Jōkyū|en|Jōkyū|WD=Q1195428|lt=Jōkyū}} 1, 26th day of the 1st month),Gregorian date obtained directly from the original Nengō using [https://uni-tuebingen.de/geschichte-japans/nengo_calc.htm Nengocalc] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930014735/http://www.uni-tuebingen.de/geschichte-japans/nengo_calc.htm |date=2007-09-30 }} shōgun [[Minamoto no Sanetomo]] was coming down from Tsurugaoka Hachimangū's Senior Shrine after assisting to a ceremony celebrating his nomination to [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]]. His nephew [[:en:Kugyō (Minamoto no Yoshinari)|Kugyō]], son of second shōgun [[Minamoto no Yoriie]], came out from next to the stone stairway of the shrine, then suddenly attacked and assassinated him in the hope to become ''{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}'' himself.Azuma Kagami; Mutsu (1995/06: 102–104) The killer is often described as hiding behind the giant ginkgo, but no contemporary text mentions the tree, and this detail is likely an {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo-period}} invention first appeared in {{ill|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|en|Tokugawa Mitsukuni|WD=Q1194944|lt=Tokugawa Mitsukuni}}'s {{ill|Shinpen Kamakurashi|en|Shinpen Kamakurashi|WD=Q2397169|lt=Shinpen Kamakurashi}}. For his act Kugyō was himself beheaded a few hours later, thus bringing the {{ill|Seiwa Genji|en|Seiwa Genji|WD=Q2164991|lt=Seiwa Genji}} line of the Minamoto clan and their rule in Kamakura to a sudden end. === Shrine and temple === [[File:Turu h kei.jpg|thumb|left|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū and the ''dankazura'' during the Edo period. Clearly visible its many Buddhist temples, later destroyed. In the lower right corner, tiny [[Moto Hachiman]]]]Tsurugaoka Hachimangū is now just a Shinto shrine but, for the almost 700 years from its foundation until the {{nihongo|''Shinto and Buddhism Separation Order''|神仏判然令}} of 1868, its name was {{nihongo|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū-ji|鶴岡八幡宮寺}} and it was also a Buddhist temple, one of the oldest in Kamakura. The mixing of Buddhism and ''kami'' worship in shrine-temple complexes like Tsurugaoka called ''{{ill|Jingū-ji|en|Jingū-ji|WD=Q1074971|lt=Jingū-ji}}'' had been normal for centuries until the Meiji government decided, for political reasons, that this was to change.[http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1110 Encyclopedia of Shinto - Shinbutsu Bunri] accessed on June 7, 2008 {{in lang|en}} (According to the ''[[honji suijaku]]'' theory, Japanese ''kami'' were just local manifestations of universal {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddhas}}, and Hachiman in particular was one of the earliest and most popular syncretic gods. Already in the 7th century, for example in {{ill|Usa, Ōita|en|Usa, Ōita|WD=Q114147|lt=Usa}}, Kyūshū, Hachiman was worshiped together with Miroku Bosatsu ([[Maitreya]]).Bernhard Scheid) The separation policy (''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'') was the direct cause of serious damage to important cultural assets. Because mixing the two religions was now forbidden, shrines and temples had to give away some of their treasures, thus damaging the integrity of their cultural heritage and decreasing the historical and economic value of their properties.Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 28) Tsurugaoka Hachiman's giant {{nihongo|{{ill|Nio (Buddhism)|en|Nio (Buddhism)|WD=Q539715|lt=Nio (Buddhism)}}|仁王}}} (the two wooden wardens usually found at the sides of a temple's entrance), being objects of Buddhist worship and therefore illegal where they were, had to be sold to {{ill|Jufuku-ji|en|Jufuku-ji|WD=Q167087|lt=Jufuku-ji}}, where they still are.See article {{ill|Jufuku-ji|en|Jufuku-ji|WD=Q167087|lt=Jufuku-ji}}Mutsu (1995/06:174) The shrine also had to destroy Buddhism-related buildings, for example its {{nihongo|[[shichidō garan]]|七堂伽藍}} (a complete seven-building Buddhist temple compound), its ''[[tahōtō]]'' tower, and its {{nihongo|''midō''|御堂|enshrinement hall (of a {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=buddha}})}}. In important ways, Tsurugaoka Hachimangū was impoverished in 1868 as a consequence of this Meiji Era policy. The imposed, inflexible reform orthodoxy of this early Meiji period was unquestionably intended to affect Buddhism and Shinto. However, the structures and artwork of this ancient shrine-temple were not yet construed as important elements of Japan's cultural patrimony.After 1897 when the ''Law for the Preservation of Ancient Shrines and Temples'' was enacted, a range of other factors would come to be considered. What remains to be visited today is only a partial version of the original shrine-temple. ===Meiji-Showa periods=== From 1871 through 1946, Tsurugaoka was officially designated one of the {{nihongo|''[[:en:Kokuhei-chūsha|Kokuhei-chūsha]]''|国幣中社}}, meaning that it stood in the mid-range of [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto Shrines|Ranked, nationally significant shrines]]. == Layout of shrine complex == [[File:TsurugaokaHachiman-M8808.jpg|thumb|left|Torii at entrance to shrine. The arched bridge is visible to the right.]] Both the shrine and the city were built with [[:en:Feng Shui|Feng Shui]] in mind. The present location was carefully chosen as the most propitious after consulting a [[:en:Diviner|Diviner]] because it had a mountain to the north (the {{nihongo|''Hokuzan''|北山}}), a river to the east (the [[Namerikawa (Kanagawa)|Namerikawa]]), a great road to the west (the {{nihongo|''Kotō Kaidō''|古東街道}}) and was open to the south (on {{ill|Sagami Bay|en|Sagami Bay|WD=Q1061221|lt=Sagami Bay}}).Ōnuki (2008:80) Each direction was protected by a god: [[:en:Black Tortoise|Genbu]] guarded the north, {{ill|Azure Dragon|en|Azure Dragon|WD=Q515882|lt=Seiryū}} the east, [[:en:White Tiger (Chinese constellation)|Byakko]] the west and {{ill|Vermilion Bird|en|Vermilion Bird|WD=Q1059392|lt=Suzaku}} the south. The [[:en:Willows|Willows]] near the Genpei Ponds (see below) and the [[catalpa]]s next to the [http://www.moma.pref.kanagawa.jp/en/public/HallTop.do?hl=k Museum of Modern Art] represent respectively Seiryū and Byakko. In spite of all the changes the shrine has gone through over the years, in this respect Yoritomo's design is still basically intact. [[File:Tsurugaoka Hachimangu From Third Torii until First Torii.jpg|thumb|Three large torii on the approach (sandō) of shrine]] There is a 1.8 km straight street in the front of shrine, called "{{ill|Wakamiya Ōji|en|Wakamiya Ōji|WD=Q7960797|lt=Wakamiya Ōji}} (若宮大路)". It is the approach ({{ill|Sandō|en|Sandō|WD=Q667783|lt=Sandō}} (参道)) of Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū, there are three big [[Torii]] (Shinto gate). The Torii gate farthest from the shrine is called Ichi-no-Torii (the first torii), the one in the middle is Ni-no-Torii (the second torii) and the one in front of the shrine is [[Wakamiya Ōji#San no Torii|San-no-Torii]] (the third torii). As one enters, after San-no-Torii (the third torii) there are three small bridges, two flat ones on the sides and an arched one at the center. In the days of the shogunate there used to be only two, a normal one and another arched, made in wood and painted red. The shōgun would leave his retinue there and proceed alone on foot to the shrine.Mutsu (1995/06: 102-104) The arched bridge was called ''Akabashi'' (''Red Bridge''), and was reserved to him: common people had to use the flat one. The bridges span over a canal that joins two ponds popularly called {{nihongo|''Genpei-ike''|源平池}}, or "Genpei ponds". The term comes from the names of the two families, the Minamoto ("Gen") and the Taira ("Pei"), that fought each other in Yoritomo's day. The stele just after and to the left of the first ''torii'' explains the origin of the name:Original Japanese text available [http://www.kcn-net.org/sisekihi/genpei.htm here]
The Genpei Ponds
File:Genpei-ike 01.JPG|Genpei ponds (Minamoto Pond) File:Genpei-ike 02.JPG|Genpei ponds (Taira Pond) The Azuma Kagami says that "In April 1182 Minamoto no Yoritomo told monk Senkō and Ōba Kageyoshi to have two ponds dug within the shrine." According to another version of the story, it was Yoritomo's wife {{ill|Hōjō Masako|en|Hōjō Masako|WD=Q463961|lt=Masako}} who, to pray for the prosperity of the Minamoto family, had these ponds dug, and had white lotuses planted in the east one and red ones in the west one, colors which are those of the Taira and Minamoto clans. From this derives their name.
The red of those lotuses is supposed to stand for the spilled blood of the Taira.Kamiya (2008: 17 - 23) ===Sub-shrines and infrastructures=== [[File:Yui-Wakamiya.jpg|thumb|The Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo, where one can pray at [[:en:Yui Wakamiya|Yui Wakamiya]] without actually going there.]] [[File:Maiden stage.jpg|thumb|left|Music performance at ''Maiden'']] Tsurugaoka Hachimangū includes several sub-shrines, the most important of which are the Junior Shrine ({{nihongo|''Wakamiya''|若宮}}) at the bottom, and the Senior Shrine ({{nihongo|''Hongū''|本宮}}) 61 steps above. The present Senior Shrine building was constructed in 1828 by {{ill|Tokugawa Ienari|en|Tokugawa Ienari|WD=Q439717|lt=Tokugawa Ienari}}, the 11th [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa]] ''shōgun'' in the ''{{ill|Hachiman-zukuri|en|Hachiman-zukuri|WD=Q3125455|lt=Hachiman-zukuri}}'' style.{{cite book|last=Bocking|first=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto - 'Hachiman-zukuri' |year=1997|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-7007-1051-5}} Right under the stairway there's an open pavilion called {{nihongo|''Maiden''|舞殿}} where weddings, dances and music are performed. A couple of hundred meters to the right of the Junior Shrine lies {{nihongo|''Shirahata Jinja''|Shirahata Shrine}}, a {{ill|National Treasure (Japan)|en|National Treasure (Japan)|WD=Q1139795|lt=National Treasure}}. To the left of the Senior Shrine lies {{nihongo|''Maruyama'' {{ill|Inari shrine|en|Inari shrine|WD=Q514480|lt=Inari shrine}}|丸山稲荷社}} with its many ''torii''. Near ''Shirahata Jinja'' one can also find the {{nihongo|''Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo''|由比若宮遥拝所}}, literally the "Yui Wakamiya Pray-at-a-Distance Place" (see photo). This facility, originally created for the ''shōgun'''s benefit, allows one to worship at distant [[:en:Yui Wakamiya|Yui Wakamiya]] ([[Moto Hachiman]]) without actually going all the way to {{ill|Zaimokuza|en|Zaimokuza|WD=Q121432378|lt=Zaimokuza}}.[http://www.kcn-net.org/e_kama_history/komachi_yukinoshita/area1_1.htm Komachi, Nishi Mikado], by the Kamakura Citizen's Network, retrieved on July 23, 2008 Right next to the ''Yui Wakamiya Yōhaijo'' there are two stones: pouring water on them should reveal on each the contour of a turtle. One of the islands in the Minamoto pond hosts a sub-shrine called {{nihongo|''Hataage Benzaiten'' Shrine|旗上弁財天社}} dedicated to goddess [[Benzaiten]], a Buddhist deity. For this reason, the sub-shrine was dismantled in 1868 at the time of the "Shinto and Buddhism separation" order (see below) and rebuilt in 1956. ===Wakamiya Ōji=== [[File:Cherry-Blossoms-Kamakura.jpg|thumb|200 px|The ''dankazura'' and its cherry trees in full bloom]]{{main|Wakamiya Ōji}} An unusual feature of the shrine is its 1.8 km {{nihongo|{{ill|Sandō|en|Sandō|WD=Q667783|lt=Sandō}}|参道}} (approach), which extends all the way to the ocean in {{ill|Yuigahama|en|Yuigahama|WD=Q8060490|lt=Yuigahama}} and doubles as Wakamiya Ōji Avenue, Kamakura's main street. Built by [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] as an imitation of Kyoto's {{nihongo|Suzaku Ōji|朱雀大路}}, Wakamiya Ōji used to be much wider and flanked by both a 3 m deep canal and pine trees (see Edo period print below).Kamakura Shōkō Kaigijo (2008: 56-57) Walking from the beach toward the shrine one passes through three ''[[torii]]'', or Shinto gates, called respectively ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#Ichi no Torii|Ichi no Torii]]'' (first gate), ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#Ni no Torii|Ni no Torii]]'' (second gate) and ''[[Wakamiya Ōji#San no Torii|San no Torii]]'' (third gate). Between the first and the second lies {{nihongo|[[Wakamiya Ōji#Geba Yotsukado|Geba Yotsukado]]|下馬四つ角}} which, as the name indicates, was the place where riders had to get off their horses in deference to [[Hachiman]] and his shrine. Some hundred meters further, between the second and third ''torii'', begins the {{nihongo|''dankazura''|段葛}}, a raised pathway flanked by cherry trees. The ''dankazura'' becomes gradually wider so that, seen from the shrine, it will look longer than it really is. The entire length of the dankazura is under the direct administration of the shrine. ===Giant ginkgo=== [[File:Giant Ginkgo in Tsurugaoka Hachiman Shrine.jpg|thumb|left|The giant ginkgo before its uprooting]] [[File:Ginkgo-reborn-2.jpg|right|thumb|The stump of the fallen ginkgo has produced leaves]] The {{ill|Ginkgo biloba|en|Ginkgo biloba|WD=Q43284|lt=ginkgo}} tree that stood next to Tsurugaoka Hachimangū's stairway almost from its foundation and which appears in almost every old print of the shrine was completely uprooted and greatly damaged at 4:40 in the morning on March 10, 2010. According to an expert who analyzed the tree, the fall is likely due to rot. Both the tree's stump and a section of its trunk replanted nearby have produced leaves (see photo). The tree was nicknamed {{nihongo|''kakure-ichō''|隠れ銀杏|hiding ginkgo}} because according to an {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} {{ill|Urban legend|en|Urban legend|WD=Q189349|lt=Urban legend}}, a now-famous assassin hid behind it before striking his victim. For details, see the article {{ill|Shinpen Kamakurashi|en|Shinpen Kamakurashi|WD=Q2397169|lt=Shinpen Kamakurashi}}. ==Activities== [[File:Kamakura Yabusame.jpg|thumb|''Yabusame'' at Tsurugaoka Hachimangū]] Tsurugaoka Hachimangū is the center of much cultural activity and both ''[[yabusame]]'', (archery from horseback), and ''[[kyūdō]]'' (Japanese archery) are practiced within the shrine. It also has extensive {{ill|Peony|en|Peony|WD=Q147105|lt=Peony}} gardens, three coffee shops, a kindergarten, offices and a ''[[:en:Dōjō|Dōjō]]''. Within its grounds stand two museums, the {{ill|Kamakura Museum of National Treasures|en|Kamakura Museum of National Treasures|WD=Q3330314|lt=Kamakura Museum of National Treasures}}, owned by the City of Kamakura, and the prefectural [http://www.moma.pref.kanagawa.jp/en/public/HallTop.do?hl=k Museum of Modern Art]. ==Gallery of shrines== File:Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū Shrine.jpg|Tsurugaoka Hachimangū – a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} with {{ill|Buddhist architecture|en|Buddhist architecture|WD=Q2047562|lt=Buddhist architecture}} File:Inner court of Tsurugaoka
